sentences: It is night. Behind a lattice window, a room glows with light.
Finely dressed women sit inside the brightness, while out in the dark, men peer in through the bars.
This is Night Scene in the Yoshiwara, painted by Katsushika Ōi.
It is a small painting, 26.
3 centimetres high and 39.
8 centimetres wide.
It is not a print but a nikuhitsu-ga, a one-of-a-kind picture painted directly by the artist's own brush.
It belongs to the Ota Memorial Museum of Art in Tokyo.
Ōi was a daughter of the great ukiyo-e master Hokusai.
Her dates of birth and death are not known, and only a dozen or so works by her have been confirmed.
Even so, her pictures, quite unlike her father's, continue to fascinate people.
Look inside the lattice.
The lamps of the room light up the women, so the colours and patterns of their robes float out of the darkness.
The museum describes the work as a masterpiece painted in light and shadow.
Find the woman who has come up close to the lattice.
Perhaps a regular customer has arrived.
Her face is drawn only as a black silhouette, so we cannot read her expression.
By showing us nothing, the painter holds our gaze all the more.
Now look outside the lattice, at the paper lanterns in the visitors' hands.
Each figure holding a lantern is lit on one side and sinks into darkness on the other.
These many small sources of light call people out of the dark here and there, like figures in a dream.
There is no signature on this painting.
Instead, characters are hidden on three lanterns.
The large lantern on the right carries the character ō, the lantern of the man in the centre carries i, and the long lantern held by a man in a hood carries Ei.
Put ō and i together and you have her art name, Ōi, while Ei is her real name, O-Ei.
So the three characters are read as a hidden signature, left quietly inside the picture.
The painting first appears in the record in a magazine of 1929, but after 1946 it vanished from view.
Only in 1982 was it reported again, having been sheltered from the war in an old family house in Okayama.
Today it belongs to the Ota Memorial Museum of Art.
The museum does not keep it on permanent view.
In the autumn of 2026 it was shown again for the first time in three years, at an exhibition tracing how ukiyo-e artists painted the night.
Step back and look again: a bright room, a dark street, and the lattice between them.
If you find yourself looking at a lit window tonight, imagine the stories on either side of it.
